name: AI for Fundraising and Grant Writing
objectives: Given one of your programs, find at least two grant opportunities that fit it, using Grants.gov, Candid or local funders, with eligibility checked in each notice

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding grants that fit your mission
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find at least two grant opportunities that fit one of your programs.
This lesson builds toward: Given one of your programs, you will find at least two grant opportunities that fit it, using Grants.gov, Candid or local funders, with eligibility checked in each notice.
Grants come from three main places: government (federal, state and local), private and family foundations, and companies. Federal grants are listed on Grants.gov. Each one has a notice of funding opportunity, or NOFO, with a section that says who is eligible.
To apply for federal grants your organization must first register as an entity in SAM.gov, which gives you a Unique Entity ID (UEI). Grants.gov says registration is free. It can take time, so start early, and never pay a company that says it will register you for a fee.
For foundations, Candid (candid.org) lets you search nonprofits and funders; some features need a paid plan, and many public libraries offer access. Also check your community foundation, local businesses and your denomination or faith network.
Step by step:
- Pick one program that needs funding.
- Search Grants.gov for federal opportunities in that area.
- Search Candid and your community foundation for local funders.
- Read each opportunity's eligibility section.
- Write down two that fit, with their deadlines.
Words to know:
- Grant: money given for a purpose that does not have to be paid back.
- NOFO: notice of funding opportunity: the official description of a federal grant and its rules.
- UEI: Unique Entity ID: the number SAM.gov gives your organization for federal awards.
Official sources:
- Grants.gov: grant eligibility
- Grants.gov: applicant registration
- SAM.gov
- Candid
Try it now: Choose one of your programs. Find two grant opportunities that fit it, one federal or state and one foundation or local. Write each funder's name, deadline and eligibility in one line.
You can now find grant opportunities that fit your mission and know what registration federal grants need.

check.q: What are the three main sources of grants?
check.why: Grants come from government, private and family foundations, and companies.

check.q: You want to search foundations on Candid but cannot afford a paid plan. What can you try?
options: Ask your public library, since many offer access
Pay a stranger for a list
Ask AI to list every foundation
check.why: Many public libraries offer access to Candid's paid features.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Reading funder guidelines with AI's help
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a funder's guidelines into a checklist of what you must submit.
This lesson builds toward: Given a funder's public guidelines, you will create a checklist of every section, limit, attachment and deadline with AI help, checked line by line against the funder's own document.
Every funder says what it wants: sections, word limits, budget format, attachments and deadlines. Missing one can disqualify you before anyone reads your work.
Guidelines are public, so you can paste them into an AI assistant and ask: "Turn these grant guidelines into a checklist: every section, its word or page limit, every attachment, and every deadline."
Then check the checklist against the original. AI can drop an item or change a date. The funder's own document always wins.
Step by step:
- Copy the funder's public guidelines.
- Ask the AI for a checklist of sections, limits, attachments and deadlines.
- Compare the checklist line by line with the original.
- Fix anything missing or wrong.
Words to know:
- Guidelines: the funder's rules for what to submit and how.
- Attachment: an extra document you send with the application, like a budget or IRS letter.
Try it now: Take the guidelines for one of your two opportunities. Ask an AI assistant for a checklist, then check it against the original and fix any mistakes.
You can now turn funder guidelines into an accurate submission checklist.

check.q: Why can you paste a funder's guidelines into an AI assistant?
options: Because AI tools are always private
Because AI will submit for you
check.why: Guidelines are public, so pasting them in shares nothing private.

check.q: AI's checklist says the deadline is March 15, but the guidelines say March 1. What do you do?
options: Ask AI again until it agrees
Use March 1, from the funder's document
check.why: AI can change a date; the funder's own document always wins.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Drafting a statement of need and program description
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft a statement of need and program description from your own facts.
This lesson builds toward: Given your own facts and checked sources, you will draft a statement of need and a program description with AI, with every number tracing to your records or a source you checked.
The statement of need says what problem you address, who is affected, and why now. The program description says what you will do, for whom, and what will change.
Give the AI your facts, not a blank page: "Using only these facts, draft a 250-word statement of need for a grant to [funder type]: [your facts and sourced statistics]. Do not add any statistics I did not give you."
Then edit hard. Add a real story (with permission, no identifying details), match the funder's words and priorities, and make sure every number traces to your records or a source you checked. Many funders ask whether AI was used; answer honestly.
Step by step:
- Gather your facts: who you serve, numbers, outcomes, sourced statistics.
- Ask AI to draft using only those facts, within the word limit.
- Add a real story with permission and no identifying details.
- Match the funder's priorities and words.
- Trace every number to a record or source.
Words to know:
- Statement of need: the grant section explaining the problem and why it matters now.
- Program description: the section explaining what you will do and what will change.
- Outcome: the change in people's lives your program aims for.
Try it now: Gather five facts about one program. Ask AI to draft a 250-word statement of need using only those facts. Mark every number and confirm where it came from.
You can now draft a grant statement of need with AI from your own checked facts.

check.q: What does a program description say?
options: What you will do, for whom, and what will change
check.why: A program description says what you will do, for whom and what will change.

check.q: You want to add a family's story to your statement of need. What do you do?
options: Use their full name to make it real
Get permission and remove identifying details
Copy a story from another group
check.why: A real story needs permission and no identifying details.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a donor appeal with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draft a short donor appeal email for one program.
This lesson builds toward: For one program, you will write a short donor appeal email with one story, what a gift does and one clear ask, with placeholders instead of donor details.
A good appeal is short and specific: one person or need, what a gift does, and one clear ask. "$50 provides a week of after-school tutoring" works better than "please support our work", but only if the number is true.
Prompt: "Write a 150-word donor appeal email for our after-school tutoring program. Tell a short story about [a student, no name], say what [amount] provides, and end with one clear ask and a link: [donate link]. Warm, hopeful tone."
Keep donor lists, names and gift histories out of the AI tool. Use your donor database or email program to add names after the draft is final.
Step by step:
- Choose one program and one true "what a gift does" fact.
- Ask AI for a short appeal with a story, the gift fact and one ask.
- Check every amount against your budget.
- Add names through your donor database, not the AI tool.
Words to know:
- Appeal: a request asking people to give.
- Call to action: the one clear thing you ask the reader to do, like "Give today".
Try it now: Draft a 150-word appeal email for one program with AI. Check that the "what a gift does" amount is true from your budget.
You can now draft a short, honest donor appeal with AI.

check.q: How many asks should a good appeal have?
check.why: A good appeal has one person or need, what a gift does and one clear ask.

check.q: You want AI to write an appeal to your top donors by name. What do you do?
options: Paste your donor list into AI
Write the draft with placeholders, then add names in your donor database
check.why: Keep donor lists out of AI; add names in your database after the draft is final.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Personalizing thank-yous and updates
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Use AI to make thank-you and update templates you personalize yourself.
This lesson builds toward: Given different kinds of donors, you will create thank-you templates with placeholders that you personalize yourself, with names and amounts added only in your donor database or mail merge.
Donors who are thanked quickly and told what their gift did are more likely to give again. AI can help you write templates for different donors: first-time givers, monthly givers, volunteers who also give, and church members who gave to a special offering.
Ask: "Write three short thank-you templates: first-time donor, monthly donor, and major donor. Each under 100 words, warm, with [name], [amount] and [program] placeholders and one sentence of impact."
Fill in names and amounts in your donor database or mail merge. Add a hand-written line when you can. People can tell when no human was involved.
Step by step:
- List the types of donors you thank.
- Ask AI for a template for each, with placeholders.
- Add a true impact sentence to each.
- Personalize in your donor database and add a personal line.
Words to know:
- Template: a reusable draft with blanks to fill in.
- Mail merge: a tool that fills names and details into a letter for many people.
- Donor retention: keeping donors giving year after year.
Try it now: Ask AI for three thank-you templates for three donor types. Add one true impact sentence to each.
You can now create thank-you templates with AI and personalize them safely.

check.q: Which donors are more likely to give again?
options: Donors thanked quickly and told what their gift did
Donors who get the same letter as everyone
check.why: Quick thanks and a report on what the gift did make donors more likely to give again.

check.q: You have a thank-you template ready for a monthly donor. What makes it feel human?
options: Adding a hand-written line when you can
check.why: People can tell when no human was involved; a hand-written line helps.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Checking, editing and staying honest
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a final check on any grant or appeal draft before it goes out.
This lesson builds toward: Before a grant or appeal goes out, you will check every number, claim, story permission and word limit, with no invented outcomes, partners or endorsements.
Before anything goes to a funder or donor, run a final check. Every number traces to a record. Every claim is true. Every story has permission. Word limits are met. It sounds like your organization, not a robot.
Never let AI invent outcomes, partners or endorsements. A funder who finds one false claim may never trust you again.
Read it out loud, and ask one colleague who knows the program to read it. For legal or tax statements, such as what is tax-deductible, check with your accountant or the official IRS guidance.
Step by step:
- Trace every number to a record or source.
- Confirm each story has permission and no identifying details.
- Check word limits and required sections.
- Read it out loud.
- Ask a colleague who knows the program to review.
Words to know:
- Endorsement: a public statement of support from a person or group.
- Tax-deductible: a gift a donor may subtract from taxable income under tax rules.
Official sources:
- IRS: Charitable contributions
Try it now: Final task: for one real grant opportunity, finish your statement of need and a program description that follow the guidelines, and finish a 150-word donor appeal for the same program. Run the final check on both.
You can now produce honest, checked grant sections and donor appeals with AI's help.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Grant fit The grant does not fit the program, or eligibility was not checked. One real opportunity that fits the program, with eligibility checked. Notes a second opportunity and the deadline for each. Follows the guidelines A required section, limit or attachment is missed. Drafts follow the funder's checklist, sections and word limits. The checklist was checked line by line against the funder's document. Need and program from facts A statistic or outcome cannot be traced to a record or source. About 250-word statement of need and a program description using only checked facts. Uses the funder's words and priorities and includes a permitted story. Donor appeal No clear ask, or donor details in the prompt. About 150 words with one story, what a gift does and one clear ask, using placeholders. The amount and what it provides come from the program's real costs. Honest and in our voice An invented outcome, partner or endorsement remains. Every claim is true and both pieces sound like the organization. A colleague who knows the program has read and approved it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a good way to catch a draft that sounds like a robot?
check.why: Read it out loud and ask a colleague who knows the program to read it.

check.q: Your grant draft says you served 300 youth, but no record shows that. What do you do?
options: Ask AI where it got the number
Remove it or use the number from your records
check.why: Every number must trace to a record or source.
